clue.text: Arab puts question to video game pioneer

blocks.note: Q is the standard abbreviation for question
Atari was an early maker of arcade and home video games

explanation.surface: An Arab man sets a quiz question to a veteran of the computer games industry.
explanation.walkthrough: Q is placed before ATARI: 'puts question to' reads as asking, but it simply sets one piece beside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A Qatari is a native of Qatar, a Gulf state, and so is an Arab.

clue.text: Sexually perverted cat?

blocks.note: surface reading: a description of a voyeur, someone who watches others undress
setter's reading: a male cat, a tom, that spies on people through the curtains

explanation.surface: A dubious pet is accused of sexual deviance.
explanation.walkthrough: A tom is a male cat, so a voyeur is pictured as a cat that peeps; the question mark flags the play on the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a voyeur, after the tailor in the Lady Godiva legend who spied on her ride.

clue.text: Struggle and sink, going over lake

indicators.note: one word goes over another, spreading around it on both sides

blocks.note: a ship that founders fills with water and sinks
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Someone thrashing in the water goes under as they cross a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: FOUNDER wraps around L after its first letter to give FLOUNDER; 'Struggle and sink' looks like one phrase, but 'and' only joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To flounder is to thrash about clumsily or have great difficulty, which is a kind of struggle.

clue.text: Cat rough in the stomach, being taken for a ride?

indicators.note: the stomach is the middle of the body, so only the central letters of the word are kept
something taken for a drive sits inside the vehicle, enclosed by it

blocks.note: in slang a ride is a car
the inner letters, dropping the first and last

explanation.surface: A big cat with an upset stomach is being driven somewhere, perhaps being conned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken for a ride' suggests being deceived; here it just means riding in a vehicle, and 'Cat' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cougar, also called puma or mountain lion, is a large wild feline of the Americas.

clue.text: Hard top vehicle, fast

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
apace means quickly

explanation.surface: A car advertisement boasting of a rigid roof and a quick motor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard top' looks like car jargon, but it is the definition: the shell on a creature's back.
explanation.definitionFit: A carapace is the hard upper shell of a tortoise, crab or beetle, literally a hard covering on top.

clue.text: Spurn one comic, a victim of cancel culture?

indicators.note: something comic is absurd or ridiculous, so the letters are arranged in a silly new way

blocks.note: the letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: A comedian who has been shunned is held up as a casualty of cancel culture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic' reads as a noun, a comedian, but it is the anagram signal. The question mark covers a modern gloss on an Orwellian word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four an unperson is someone erased from record, much as cancel culture is said to erase people.

clue.text: 'Nobel Prize winner!' editor screamed

blocks.note: Saul Bellow won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1976
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An editor shouts excitedly that a writer has won the Nobel Prize.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation marks make it seem a quoted cry; in fact the laureate's surname is the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To bellow is to shout loudly and deeply, so bellowed works as a past-tense synonym for screamed.

clue.text: Notice among those making jam it doesn't always flow

indicators.note: being among others means being placed in their midst, surrounded by them

blocks.note: the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation famous for jam-making
an ad is a notice in a newspaper

explanation.surface: A poster is put up among jam-makers, about something that will not always flow, like the conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute is a British organisation known for jam and cakes; the setter refers to its members as those making jam.
explanation.definitionFit: A wadi is a desert valley or watercourse that is dry except in the rainy season, so its stream runs only intermittently.

clue.text: Poet recited and finished

indicators.note: a poem recited is spoken, so we work from the spoken form of the name

blocks.note: John Donne, the English metaphysical poet, whose name is said 'dun'

explanation.surface: A poet performed a reading and then was done.
explanation.definitionFit: Done means completed or over, a direct synonym for finished.

clue.text: Ring again to cancel

blocks.note: first meaning: to sound the bells once more
second meaning: to revoke a law

explanation.surface: Someone phones a second time to call off a booking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring again' suggests a phone call; the word is split as RE (again) plus PEAL, a ringing of bells.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament repeals an act when it revokes it, which is to cancel the law.

clue.text: Smoking area I sound hesitant to install in work room

indicators.note: installing something places it inside a structure, here between the other two parts

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a work
taken as written
um is the noise of hesitating
a den is a small private room

explanation.surface: A worker hesitantly suggests putting a smoking area in the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work room' looks like one place, an office, but it is two separate words, with the hesitant 'I' placed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: An opium den was a place where people went to smoke the drug, so a smoking area of a notorious kind.

clue.text: Cut up into fragments, had jolly time collecting them

indicators.note: a word broken into fragments has its pieces scattered and reassembled
collecting something gathers it in, so the earlier pieces go inside

blocks.note: partied means celebrated, had fun
the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Something was smashed to bits, and someone had a great time picking up the pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a mere linking preposition, but it is the fodder, and 'them' points back to its scrambled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Partitioned means divided into separate sections, which is what cutting something up does.

clue.text: Popular national hero back injecting portion of drug, liable to be charged

indicators.note: going back means travelling the wrong way, so the name runs right to left
injecting puts something inside, as a needle does

blocks.note: in means fashionable, popular
El Cid, the medieval Castilian warrior, is Spain's national hero
a tab is a single tablet, a dose of a drug

explanation.surface: A celebrated hero caught taking drugs could face prosecution.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed hero splits around the drug: DIC-TAB-LE, after IN. The drug scandal makes 'drug' look literal.
explanation.definitionFit: An indictable offence is one for which a person can be formally accused and tried in court.

clue.text: Strut around the Parisian stage at last, dancing in this

indicators.note: one word goes around another, enclosing it
at last points to the final letter of the word only

blocks.note: to swank is to swagger or show off
la is French for 'the' (feminine)
the final letter only

explanation.surface: A performer struts about the Paris stage, finally dancing in this production.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the end of the clue, a work one dances in; 'Strut around' looks like a phrase, but around is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Swan Lake is Tchaikovsky's ballet, the classic work dancers perform on stage.

clue.text: Weight of cereal nearly filled with half of essential nutrients

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
only half the word survives; the second half is cut away
something filled has other material packed inside it

blocks.note: cereal crops such as wheat and oats are grasses
vitamins are nutrients the body needs

explanation.surface: A nutritional label on a cereal box: weight, and vitamin content.
explanation.walkthrough: GRAS (most of grass) is filled with VITA (first half of vitamins). The breakfast-cereal picture hides that 'Weight' means seriousness.
explanation.definitionFit: Gravitas is dignity or seriousness, and weight in the sense of importance, as in 'his opinion carries weight'.

clue.text: Carrying papa colt moved easily, but noisily?

definitions.text: Carrying papa colt moved easily, but noisily?

indicators.note: carrying something means having it held within

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for colt in horse-racing form
to lope is to move with an easy, long stride
Papa is the NATO alphabet word for P

explanation.surface: A horse bearing its sire trotted along comfortably, though with a clatter.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes inside LOPED, after C. The whole clue then describes the answer: a young horse moving along with noisy hoofbeats.
explanation.definitionFit: To clop is to make the hollow clatter of hooves on a hard road, so the colt moved noisily.

clue.text: Caver moving right into opening for light

indicators.note: moving the letter takes it out of its place at the end
into shows where the moved letter is set down, inside the remainder

blocks.note: a potholer explores caves
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A caver heads toward a gap where daylight shines through.
explanation.walkthrough: Potholing is the British word for caving. The final letter of the caver shifts forward to sit after the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A porthole is a small round window in a ship's side, letting in light.

clue.text: Confrontation between gangs over some grass?

blocks.note: first meaning: gangs fighting for control of territory
second, playful meaning: a literal fight about a patch of lawn, sods of grass

explanation.surface: Rival gangs square up, maybe about drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Grass could suggest cannabis; the joke is that the gangs fight over lawn, the literal meaning of their territory.
explanation.definitionFit: A gang's patch is its territory, and a conflict between gangs over control of it is the standard phrase.

clue.text: Vain monarch made out as a virtuoso pianist

indicators.note: something made out is interpreted or deciphered, so the letters must be worked into a new order

blocks.note: the letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: A conceited king fancies himself a great pianist.
explanation.definitionFit: Sergei Rachmaninov, the Russian composer, was one of the greatest concert pianists of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Herald of rain coming up in under a minute

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: sub is Latin for under, as in submarine
MIN is the abbreviation for minute

explanation.surface: A warning that rain is on its way in less than a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up in under a minute' reads as a time frame; it tells us SUB and MIN are read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A nimbus is a dark rain-bearing cloud, so its arrival heralds rain.

clue.text: Reporter's hunt for Punjabi perhaps

indicators.note: a reporter speaks on air, so the word is taken as it is spoken

blocks.note: to seek is to hunt for

explanation.surface: A journalist goes in search of someone from the Punjab.
explanation.definitionFit: Sikhism began in the Punjab and most Sikhs live there, so a Sikh is an example of a Punjabi.

clue.text: Cross, I say no every so often in ancient capital

indicators.note: every so often means at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: X is the shape of a cross
taken as written
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: An annoyed visitor keeps refusing things in an old capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Xi'an in China was the capital of several dynasties and is home to the Terracotta Army.

clue.text: One PM, short bloke, EU citizen

indicators.note: short means cut down, so the last letter is lopped off

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
Rishi Sunak, UK prime minister 2022 to 2024
a bloke is a man

explanation.surface: A list of people: a prime minister, a small man, and a European.
explanation.walkthrough: PM is the Prime Minister, here Rishi Sunak, used by first name and cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland is a member of the European Union, so an Irishman is a citizen of the EU.

clue.text: It's doubly dotty to write in German

definitions.text: It's doubly dotty to write in German

blocks.note: surface reading: twice as crazy, mad to attempt
setter's reading: a mark of two dots written over vowels in German

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that writing in German is doubly mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Dotty means crazy; read literally it means having dots, two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the diacritic of two dots placed over a vowel in German, as in ü, showing a change in sound.

clue.text: Capital's sweetheart, old Scottish singer

blocks.note: hon is short for honey, a term of endearment
O is the abbreviation for old
Lulu is a Scottish pop singer, famous for 'Shout'

explanation.surface: A city's beloved is an elderly singer from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Lulu is a Scottish pop singer, known in Britain since the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: Honolulu, on Oahu, is the state capital of Hawaii.

clue.text: Force's uniform concealed by gown

indicators.note: something concealed by a garment is covered and held inside it

blocks.note: a gown is a dress
Uniform is the NATO alphabet word for U

explanation.surface: A police or army uniform is hidden under a long dress.
explanation.walkthrough: U goes inside DRESS after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress is coercion by threats, so action under duress is taken by force.
